title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Intermediate microeconomics hands you a pile of results that look unrelated: Shephard’s Lemma, Hotelling’s Lemma, Roy’s Identity. Each gets its own proof, its own diagram, its own place on the exam.
They are the same theorem. Once you see the envelope theorem, the other three are one-line substitutions.

title: Why Substitution Doesn’t Save You Money (At First)
text:
Why this feels wrong
The intuition that substitution should help isn’t wrong — it’s just second-order. Here’s the cleanest way to see it.
Fix a consumption bundle \(x^{(k)}\) and ask what it costs as \(p_1\) varies. The answer is \(p \cdot x^{(k)}\), which is a straight line in \(p_1\) with slope \(x_1^{(k)}\). Every possible bundle gives you one such line.
The expenditure function is the lower envelope of all these lines: at each price, you pick whichever bundle is cheapest. So \(e(p_1, u)\) is the minimum over a family of straight lines — which makes it concave, and which means at any given price it’s tangent to whichever line is currently optimal.
Tangent means same slope. The slope of that line is \(x_1^*\). Hence Shephard.

library(ggplot2)

# Cobb-Douglas u = x1^a * x2^(1-a), target utility u = 1
a <- 0.5
u_target <- 1
p2 <- 1

# True expenditure function: e(p1,p2,u) = u * (p1/a)^a * (p2/(1-a))^(1-a)
e_true <- function(p1) u_target * (p1/a)^a * (p2/(1-a))^(1-a)

# Hicksian demand for good 1: h1 = a*e/p1
h1 <- function(p1) a * e_true(p1) / p1

p_grid <- seq(0.5, 4, length.out = 200)

# Cost of holding the bundle that was optimal at price p0, as p1 varies
fixed_bundle_line <- function(p0) {
  x1 <- h1(p0)
  x2 <- (1 - a) * e_true(p0) / p2
  data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = p_grid * x1 + p2 * x2, anchor = p0)
}

anchors <- c(0.75, 1.25, 2, 3)
lines_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(anchors, fixed_bundle_line))
env_df   <- data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = e_true(p_grid))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = lines_df,
            aes(p1, cost, group = anchor),
            colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = env_df, aes(p1, cost), linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = expression(p[1]), y = "Expenditure") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







Figure 1: The expenditure function as the lower envelope of fixed-bundle cost lines. Grey lines are the cost of holding a fixed bundle; the black curve is the cost of optimally re-choosing at every price.





Each grey line is a rigid consumer who never adjusts. The black curve is you, re-optimising constantly. Notice that where a grey line touches the black curve, they don’t just meet — they graze. The gap opens up quadratically, not linearly.
That’s the resolution. Substitution does save you money. It just saves you an amount proportional to \((\Delta p)^2\), which vanishes relative to the first-order cost \(x_1 \Delta p\) when \(\Delta p\) is small. At the margin, you were already optimising, so \(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial x = 0\), and the term \(\sum_i (\partial x_i^*/\partial p_1)\) gets multiplied by zero.
This is the envelope theorem in general: when you differentiate an optimised value with respect to a parameter, you can ignore how the optimal choice shifts. Only the direct effect survives.

title: Why Substitution Doesn’t Save You Money (At First)
section: Why it matters: the CPI overstates inflation
text:
Why it matters: the CPI overstates inflation
This isn’t just a classroom curiosity. The Consumer Price Index is (roughly) a Laspeyres index: it prices a fixed basket from some base period. In the figure above, that is a grey line.
The true cost-of-living change is the black curve. Since the envelope lies weakly below every line, a fixed-basket index systematically overstates how much more expensive it has become to reach the same standard of living. This is substitution bias.

# Data: BLS Consumer Price Index, annual averages, 1982-84 = 100.
# Series CUUR0000SAF1 (Food) and CUUR0000SA0E (Energy).
# Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, https://data.bls.gov/
cpi <- data.frame(
  year   = 2019:2024,
  food   = c(255.7, 267.3, 277.7, 305.6, 322.9, 331.0),
  energy = c(212.9, 190.9, 237.0, 300.3, 285.4, 285.9)
)

# Normalise both series to 2019 = 1
cpi$p_food   <- cpi$food   / cpi$food[1]
cpi$p_energy <- cpi$energy / cpi$energy[1]

# Assume Cobb-Douglas preferences with equal shares in the base year.
# Laspeyres: cost of the 2019 basket at current prices.
cpi$laspeyres <- 0.5 * cpi$p_food + 0.5 * cpi$p_energy

# True COLI under Cobb-Douglas: geometric mean of price relatives.
cpi$true_coli <- cpi$p_food^0.5 * cpi$p_energy^0.5

plot_df <- data.frame(
  year  = rep(cpi$year, 2),
  index = c(cpi$laspeyres, cpi$true_coli),
  which = rep(c("Fixed basket (Laspeyres)", "True cost of living"),
              each = nrow(cpi))
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(year, index, colour = which)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey45", "black")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Index (2019 = 1)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 2: Fixed-basket (Laspeyres) index vs. true cost-of-living index, US food and energy CPI, 2019–2024.





The two lines track each other closely in calm years and separate when relative prices move sharply — 2021–22, when energy prices spiked while food rose more moderately. That is exactly the envelope theorem’s prediction: the bias is second-order in the size of the price change.
The stakes are not small. The 1996 Boskin Commission concluded that the CPI overstated inflation by roughly 1.1 percentage points annually, with substitution bias a major component. Since Social Security payments are indexed to the CPI, that gap compounds into hundreds of billions of dollars over a decade.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Takeaway
When you differentiate a value function, ignore how the optimal choice moves and differentiate the Lagrangian directly. That single fact gives you Shephard, Hotelling, Roy and Le Chatelier — plus the reason a small tax has deadweight loss proportional to the square of the tax. Four lemmas, one theorem, and the FOC doing all the work.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
The unconstrained case
Let \(f(x,\theta)\) be an objective function and \(\theta\) a parameter. Define the value function
\[V(\theta) = \max_{x} f(x,\theta), \qquad x^*(\theta) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x} f(x,\theta).\]
Substitute the maximiser back in and differentiate by the chain rule:
\[\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\bigg|_{x^*}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta}}_{\text{indirect effect}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x^*}}_{\text{direct effect}}.\]
At an interior maximum the first-order condition is \(\partial f/\partial x = 0\). The indirect term is therefore zero — no matter how violently \(x^*\) moves. So
\[\boxed{\;\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x = x^*(\theta)}\;}\]
Note what we never needed: \(dx^*/d\theta\) itself. It is annihilated by the FOC, which is exactly why the theorem is useful when the comparative statics of \(x^*\) are intractable.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
The constrained case
Now impose a constraint:
\[V(\theta) = \max_x f(x,\theta) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad g(x,\theta) = 0,\]
with Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda,\theta) = f(x,\theta) - \lambda\, g(x,\theta)\) and first-order conditions
\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}, \qquad g\big(x^*(\theta),\theta\big) = 0.\]
Differentiating \(V(\theta) = f(x^*(\theta),\theta)\) gives the same decomposition as before — but now the indirect term does not vanish, because \(\partial f/\partial x \neq 0\) at a constrained optimum.
The rescue comes from the constraint, which holds identically in \(\theta\). Differentiate it:
\[\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta} + \frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta} = -\frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta}.\]
Substitute the FOC \(\partial f/\partial x = \lambda\,\partial g/\partial x\) into the indirect term:
\[\frac{dV}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}=\lambda\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\frac{dx^*}{d\theta} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} - \lambda\frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{x^*,\,\lambda^*}.\]
Differentiate the Lagrangian, hold \(x\) and \(\lambda\) fixed, done. When \(g\) does not involve \(\theta\), the second term drops out and this reduces to the unconstrained formula. The multiplier earns its keep here: moving \(\theta\) also loosens or tightens the constraint, and that channel is not second-order.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Four applications
The theorem holds for minimisation too: apply the result above to \(-f\) and negate. Only the second-order conditions differ, and they play no role in the argument.
Shephard’s Lemma. Expenditure minimisation: \(e(p,\bar u) = \min_x \{p \cdot x : u(x) \ge \bar u\}\), so \(\mathcal{L} = p \cdot x - \lambda(u(x) - \bar u)\). Consider \(\theta = p_i\). Then \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial p_i = x_i\), giving
\[\frac{\partial e(p,\bar u)}{\partial p_i} = h_i(p,\bar u).\]
Take \(\theta = \bar u\) instead and \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial \bar u = \lambda\), so \(\partial e/\partial \bar u = \lambda^*\) — the multiplier is the shadow price of utility. The identical argument applied to the firm’s cost function \(c(y,w) = \min_x \{w \cdot x : F(x) \ge y\}\) gives \(\partial c/\partial w_j = x_j(y,w)\), the conditional factor demand.
Hotelling’s Lemma. Profit maximisation over inputs: \(\pi(p,w) = \max_x \{p\,F(x) - w \cdot x\}\), unconstrained. With \(f(x,p,w) = p\,F(x) - w\cdot x\), take \(\theta = p\):
\[\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\bigg|_{x^*} = F(x^*) = y^*(p,w),\]
the profit-maximising supply. Take \(\theta = w_j\) and \(\partial f/\partial w_j = -x_j\), so \(\partial\pi/\partial w_j = -x_j^*(p,w)\) — the unconditional factor demand.
Roy’s Identity. Utility maximisation: \(v(p,m) = \max_x u(x)\) s.t. \(p\cdot x = m\), so \(\mathcal{L} = u(x) - \lambda(p\cdot x - m)\). Two applications:
\[\frac{\partial v}{\partial p_i} = -\lambda x_i^*, \qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial m} = \lambda.\]
Divide one by the other and \(\lambda\) cancels:
\[x_i^*(p,m) = -\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}.\]
Marshallian demand recovered from the indirect utility function without solving the consumer’s problem again.
The Le Chatelier principle. Compare a short run with \(x_2\) fixed against a long run where it adjusts. The long-run cost function is the lower envelope of the short-run ones: they are tangent at the reference factor price \(w_1^0\), and \(c^{\mathrm{LR}}\) lies weakly below everywhere else. So \(D(w_1) = c^{\mathrm{SR}} - c^{\mathrm{LR}} \ge 0\) attains its minimum of zero at \(w_1^0\), giving \(D''(w_1^0) \ge 0\). By Shephard, \(x_1 = \partial c/\partial w_1\), so
\[\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{SR}}}{\partial w_1} \ \ge\ \frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{LR}}}{\partial w_1}.\]
Both second derivatives are non-positive because cost functions are concave in factor prices — the same envelope argument that makes \(e\) concave in \(p\). Combining this with the inequality above gives, in absolute value,
\[\left|\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{LR}}}{\partial w_1}\right| \ \ge\ \left|\frac{\partial x_1^{\mathrm{SR}}}{\partial w_1}\right|.\]
Long-run conditional demand responds at least as much as short-run. Samuelson’s 1947 result — a consequence of the geometry of optimisation, not of any additional behavioural assumption.

title: One Theorem, Four Lemmas: The Envelope Theorem in Microeconomics
text:
Why “envelope”?
The name is literal. Fix a consumption bundle \(x^{(k)}\) and ask what it costs as \(p_1\) varies: the answer is \(p \cdot x^{(k)}\), a straight line in \(p_1\) with slope \(x_1^{(k)}\). Every bundle gives one such line.
The expenditure function is the lower envelope of that family — at each price you take whichever bundle is cheapest. A minimum over straight lines is concave, and at every price it is tangent to whichever line is currently optimal. Tangent means equal slope, and that slope is \(x_1^*\). Shephard’s Lemma, read straight off the picture.


Show code
library(ggplot2)

# Cobb-Douglas: u = x1^a * x2^(1-a). All curves below are closed-form
a <- 0.5; u_target <- 1; p2 <- 1

# Expenditure function e(p1,p2,u) = u * (p1/a)^a * (p2/(1-a))^(1-a)
e_true <- function(p1) u_target * (p1/a)^a * (p2/(1-a))^(1-a)

# Hicksian demand for good 1, from Shephard: h1 = a*e/p1
h1 <- function(p1) a * e_true(p1) / p1

p_grid <- seq(0.5, 4, length.out = 200)

# Cost of the bundle that was optimal at p0, evaluated at every p1
fixed_bundle_line <- function(p0) {
  x1 <- h1(p0)
  x2 <- (1 - a) * e_true(p0) / p2
  data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = p_grid * x1 + p2 * x2, anchor = p0)
}

lines_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.75, 1.25, 2, 3), fixed_bundle_line))
env_df   <- data.frame(p1 = p_grid, cost = e_true(p_grid))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = lines_df, aes(p1, cost, group = anchor),
            colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = env_df, aes(p1, cost), linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = expression(p[1]), y = "Expenditure") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 1: Grey lines: the cost of holding one fixed bundle as \(p_1\) varies. Black curve: the cost of re-optimising at every price. The black curve is their lower envelope, and grazes each line tangentially.





Each grey line is a consumer who never adjusts. The black curve is one who re-optimises constantly. Where they touch, they graze — the gap opens quadratically, not linearly. That is the envelope theorem as a picture: at the optimum, small adjustments are free to first order.
Data. No external data. Every curve is generated from the closed-form Cobb-Douglas expenditure function in the code above; the only inputs are \(a = 0.5\), \(\bar u = 1\), \(p_2 = 1\).
